title: What carries across sports
subtitle: Which reliability comparisons are supported across NBA, MLB, soccer and tennis, and what a shared metric scale does not establish
abstract: CourtVision runs the same reliability decomposition and the same skill-score formula in more than one sport, but an identical formula run in two places does not by itself make the two results comparable. kernel_transfer.json (generated 2026-07-22) records five explicit sport/market comparability decisions and marks only two reliability_comparable: mlb moneyline_ingame (n=78,986) and soccer_intl moneyline_ingame (n=9,003), because both score a probability against a resolved binary win/loss outcome on the same 0-1 Murphy reliability scale. The other three are marked not comparable by construction, not by a measured difference: mlb totals_margin scores a run-count distribution with CRPS rather than a binary outcome (n=671); nba's win-probability benchmark stores only per-checkpoint Brier means with no reliability/resolution split computed (n=6,371); and tennis's two gate receipts compare model against model, with no market-side probability at all (n=55,075). Where the comparison is supported, the reliability gap (model minus market) has the same sign in both sports -- the model is less reliable than the market in both -- but the two gaps differ by close to 5.9-fold (0.00664 in mlb versus 0.039414 in soccer_intl), and the source file itself calls a 2-sport sign match a coincidence worth re-checking, not a pattern. cross_sport_scoreboard.json's 17 paired-delta rows mix a Brier-scale metric family (nba and soccer_intl winprob) with a CRPS-scale family (mlb margin and total-runs) inside one paired_delta_mean column; most rows are UNDERPOWERED or MARKET_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL, with three MODEL_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL exceptions confined to one mlb CRPS checkpoint family. brier_skill_scores.json's identical BSS formula returns a value below zero against the market at every grain it reports in both sports, on populations of very different size and base rate.

blocks.text: CourtVision computes the same two cross-sport statistics in more than one sport: the Murphy reliability component of a Brier score, and the Brier Skill Score (BSS) against a market reference and a climatology reference. Running an identical formula in two sports raises a question before any cross-sport reading is attempted: is the resulting number actually comparable across those sports, or does it only look comparable because the formula and the numeric scale are the same? kernel_transfer.json exists to answer that question row by row, before any transfer claim is made -- it records, for five sport/market combinations, whether the reliability axis is honestly shared, and states the reason either way.

This paper works through three things in order. First, the five comparability decisions in kernel_transfer.json: two are marked reliability_comparable, three are not, and each carries a verbatim reason rather than a judgment call made here. Second, cross_sport_scoreboard.json's 17 paired-delta rows, which use one column shape (paired_delta_mean plus a 95 percent confidence interval) across two different underlying metrics -- Brier for the win-probability rows, CRPS for the margin and total-runs rows -- and what that mixing does and does not let a reader do. Third, brier_skill_scores.json, where the identical BSS formula runs in mlb and soccer_intl on populations that differ sharply in size and base rate, to show concretely why a shared metric scale does not make two populations the same population.

kernel_transfer.json stores one row per sport/market combination under rows[], with fields sport, market, reliability_model, reliability_market, reliability_gap, reliability_unit, reliability_comparable, comparability_reason, n and sources. Its method field states the file is composition only: the reliability and resolution numbers are copied verbatim from murphy_decomposition.py and soccer_calibration_pack.py output, and the verdicts are copied or summarized verbatim from each source artifact; nothing in the file is recomputed. The file carries 5 rows (n_rows: 5) and a generated_at of 2026-07-22T22:55:23Z.

cross_sport_scoreboard.json stores 17 rows (n_rows: 17, generated_at 2026-07-22T20:15:22Z) with fields sport, market, checkpoint, n, paired_delta_mean, paired_delta_95ci and verdict, plus a source path per row. Its method field is the same composition-only statement: every number copied verbatim from its source artifact. The paired_delta_mean column is not one metric -- for the nba and soccer_intl rows it is a Brier-scale delta (from -0.1075 to +0.0019 across the file), and for the mlb_ingame and mlb_pregame rows it is a CRPS-scale delta (from -0.0523 to +1.7940), because CRPS and Brier are scored in different units. Nothing in the file's own schema flags that difference; a reader has to already know CRPS is not Brier before reading the column as one axis.

brier_skill_scores.json reports the standard BSS formula, BSS = 1 - Brier / Brier_ref, against two references (climatology and market) for two sports: mlb (n_rows 78,986, sport_base_rate 0.4563) and soccer_intl (n_rows 9,003, sport_base_rate 0.6055). Its floors field states a rule for itself -- n>=30 rows per grain before a BSS is reported -- and every grain listed for both sports carries below_floor: false, meaning that floor was met throughout this file. generated_at is 2026-07-25T11:12:35Z.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: kernel_transfer.json marks a row reliability_comparable only when both sides being compared score a probability against a resolved binary outcome using the Murphy reliability component (mean squared calibration error, weighted by bin mass) on the same 0-1 probability scale -- reliability_unit is literally the string brier_reliability_component (probability scale, 0-1) for both of the two comparable rows. Sharing that scale is a narrow, specific condition: it says the two numbers are measured the same way, nothing about the corpus, the outcome type, or the games they were measured on. A shared BSS formula or a shared 0-1 Brier scale does not by itself mean two sports' samples are matched in size, base rate or market structure, and it does not make a magnitude measured in one sport transferable to another.

Every number below is copied from kernel_transfer.json, cross_sport_scoreboard.json or brier_skill_scores.json; none is re-scored or re-estimated. Three quantities are computed here, and each is trivial arithmetic on cited fields, marked as such where it appears: the ratio of mlb to soccer_intl corpus size (78,986 / 9,003, about 8.8), the share of each sport's named brier_skill_scores.json grains that sum to its own all grain (mlb: 19,900+18,765+13,981 against 78,986; soccer_intl: 627+666+628+828+504+405 against 9,003), and the ratio of the two comparable reliability_gap values (0.039414 / 0.00664). That last ratio is not independently derived here -- kernel_transfer.json's own reliability_transfer_summary field already states it as about 5.9x, and this paper quotes that figure rather than recomputing it a second way.

The verdict labels quoted throughout (UNDERPOWERED, MARKET_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL, MODEL_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL, REPLICATED, REJECT) are copied verbatim from the source files' own verdict and comparable_groups fields; this paper does not re-run the underlying tests or re-derive a verdict from the paired_delta_mean and confidence interval columns.

blocks.note: yes/no reproduces the reliability_comparable field verbatim; reliability gap is reliability_model minus reliability_market as stored in the file, not recomputed.

items: Both comparable rows (mlb and soccer_intl moneyline_ingame) share one reason, given verbatim: both sides are Brier scores of a probability against a binary win/loss outcome -- the reliability component (mean squared calibration error, weighted by bin mass) is on the same 0-1 probability scale in both sports, the one honest cross-sport axis here.

mlb totals_margin (n=671), not comparable: CRPS scores a full run-count distribution, not a binary outcome probability -- Murphy reliability/resolution is undefined for it here; never forced onto the Brier axis above.

nba winprob_ingame (n=6,371), not comparable: nba's benchmark stores per-checkpoint Brier MEANS only -- no 10-bin Murphy reliability/resolution split has been computed locally for nba win-prob, honest gap not an estimate.

tennis pregame_prior + ingame_surface_gate (n=55,075), not comparable: both tennis gate receipts are model-vs-model checks (prior vs base; surface-specific vs surface-blind) -- no market_prob to decompose against, reliability undefined by construction.

blocks.text: Where the comparison is supported, the reliability_gap agrees in sign: the model is less reliable than the market in both mlb (+0.00664) and soccer_intl (+0.039414), each stored as reliability_model minus reliability_market. The two gaps differ by close to 5.9-fold, and kernel_transfer.json's own reliability_transfer_summary field is explicit that n=2 sports is not enough to call this a general cross-sport pattern -- a same-direction coincidence worth re-checking if a third sport gets a market-side Murphy decomposition, not a claim. This paper adds nothing beyond that reading: the honest state of the evidence is a sign match on two sports and an unexplained near-sixfold difference in magnitude.

blocks.note: Verdict labels copied verbatim from the file. CRPS-scale rows (mlb_ingame, mlb_pregame) and Brier-scale rows (nba, soccer_intl) are not on the same numeric axis -- see the caution below.

blocks.label: Caution
blocks.text: Two different metrics share one column in this table. paired_delta_mean is a Brier-scale delta for the nba and soccer_intl winprob rows (values from -0.1075 to +0.0019) and a CRPS-scale delta for the mlb_ingame and mlb_pregame rows (values from -0.0523 to +1.7940). CRPS and Brier are not the same unit -- kernel_transfer.json's own comparability_reason for mlb totals_margin states CRPS is undefined on the Murphy Brier axis used elsewhere in this paper. Reading down the paired_delta_mean column as if it were one scale, for instance treating the mlb CRPS delta of 1.7940 as a larger effect than the nba Brier delta of -0.0084, does not establish that the mlb effect is larger; it establishes only that CRPS deltas and Brier deltas are numerically different scales.

Within a metric family, most rows do not resolve in either direction. All four nba winprob checkpoints, mlb_pregame, and 9 of the 10 mlb_ingame CRPS rows are labeled UNDERPOWERED or MARKET_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL. The only MODEL_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL rows are three consecutive mlb_ingame total_runs checkpoints (end_inning_6, n=54; end_inning_7, n=55; end_inning_8, n=49), each still marked PROVISIONAL rather than settled. nba's one resolved row, end_q1 (n=1,592, paired_delta_mean -0.0084, 95 percent CI -0.0161 to -0.0008, both bounds negative), is labeled MARKET_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL; the other three nba checkpoints have confidence intervals that cross zero and are labeled UNDERPOWERED.

Two soccer_intl rows -- home_win_prob at minute_60 (n=22, paired_delta_mean -0.0931, CI -0.1570 to -0.0336) and minute_75 (n=17, paired_delta_mean -0.1075, CI -0.1885 to -0.0316) -- have confidence intervals that do not cross zero, the same shape of evidence that earns nba's end_q1 row a SHARPER label, yet both are labeled UNDERPOWERED. The file does not document the rule that assigns a SHARPER label versus UNDERPOWERED, so this paper cannot say whether n (17 and 22, well below the n>=30 floor brier_skill_scores.json applies to itself) or some other criterion produced that label; it only reports that the label and the confidence interval do not obviously agree on these two rows.

sections.heading: Results: the same BSS formula in two sports

blocks.text: Table 3 gives the BSS-vs-market figures for every grain brier_skill_scores.json reports, in both sports it covers.

blocks.caption: Brier Skill Score vs market by sport and grain, all 11 reported grains (source brier_skill_scores.json, generated 2026-07-25)
blocks.note: Do not rank the all row against its sport's named grains below it -- all is the full corpus, not a sum of the named grains (see below). Below floor reproduces the file's own below_floor field: false means the grain met its own n>=30 rule.

blocks.text: BSS against market is negative at every one of the 11 grains listed, in both sports -- from -0.0794 (mlb, early) to -0.4635 (mlb, late) within mlb, and from -0.4701 (soccer_intl, 60-75) to -1.0794 (soccer_intl, 0-15) within soccer_intl. Every listed grain in both sports carries below_floor: false, meaning each met the file's own n>=30 floor before a BSS was reported. Both sports run the identical formula (BSS = 1 - Brier / Brier_ref) against the identical kind of reference (the closing market probability), and both return a negative number nearly everywhere -- but the two sports are not otherwise alike. mlb's all grain has 78,986 rows against soccer_intl's 9,003, a ratio of about 8.8; the two sports' base rates differ (mlb 0.4563, soccer_intl 0.6055); and the named grains cover different shares of their own sport's all row -- mlb's three named grains sum to 52,646 of 78,986 rows (66.6 percent), while soccer_intl's six named minute buckets sum to 3,658 of 9,003 rows (40.6 percent). Neither sport's reported grains account for the whole corpus, and the shortfall is proportionally larger in soccer_intl.

Running the same formula on two populations of very different size, base rate and grain coverage is exactly the situation where a shared scale does not establish a shared population. The negative-against-market result is retained here as the honest outcome in both sports, not softened by that difference -- but the difference is why this paper does not treat the mlb and soccer_intl BSS-vs-market numbers as one combined finding, only as two separately measured, same-direction results.

blocks.text: BSS = 1 - Brier_model / Brier_reference; reliability_gap = reliability_model - reliability_market (Murphy decomposition, 0-1 probability scale, mlb and soccer_intl moneyline_ingame only)

sections.heading: Robustness and what would falsify this

items: If a third sport gained a market-side Murphy reliability decomposition and its reliability_gap sign disagreed with mlb and soccer_intl (model more reliable than market rather than less), the current sign-agrees-across-2-sports reading would have to be dropped as a coincidence, exactly as kernel_transfer.json's own summary already warns.

If the two soccer_intl scoreboard rows with n below 30 (minute_60, minute_75) were re-run at a materially larger n and the verdict flipped from UNDERPOWERED to a SHARPER label while the confidence interval kept excluding zero the same way, that would support n as the deciding factor behind the label; the current files do not state this rule, so it cannot be confirmed from kernel_transfer.json or cross_sport_scoreboard.json alone.

If the three mlb_ingame total_runs MODEL_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL checkpoints (end_inning_6/7/8, n=49-55) reversed sign at a larger n, that would undercut reading this three-checkpoint run as a stable in-game pattern rather than a small-sample result.

If soccer_intl's BSS-vs-market figures moved toward mlb's range (roughly -0.08 to -0.46) once the soccer_intl corpus grew well past its current 9,003 rows, that would support corpus size as part of why soccer_intl's BSS-vs-market is uniformly more negative than mlb's; at the current sample sizes this paper cannot separate a size effect from a genuine sport difference.

Only 2 of the 5 kernel_transfer.json rows support any cross-sport reliability comparison; the other 3 are excluded by construction (a different metric, no decomposition computed, or no market side), not measured and found equal -- nothing here generalizes the 2-sport reading to mlb totals, nba win-probability or tennis.

The reliability_gap sign match between mlb and soccer_intl rests on n=2 sports; kernel_transfer.json's own reliability_transfer_summary calls it a coincidence worth re-checking, not a pattern, and this paper does not treat it as more than that.

cross_sport_scoreboard.json mixes a Brier-scale metric family (nba, soccer_intl winprob) and a CRPS-scale metric family (mlb margin, mlb total_runs, mlb pregame) inside one paired_delta_mean column; comparing raw magnitudes across that boundary is not supported by the file.

Two soccer_intl scoreboard rows (n=17, n=22) have confidence intervals that exclude zero yet carry an UNDERPOWERED verdict, and the file does not document the labeling rule; this paper reports the mismatch, it does not resolve it.

brier_skill_scores.json's named grains do not sum to each sport's all row (66.6 percent of mlb rows, 40.6 percent of soccer_intl rows are covered by the named grains), so the per-grain and all-row BSS figures describe overlapping but not identical sets of games, and the all row is not a rankable additional grain alongside the named ones.
None of the three artifacts here tests why the market is more reliable, or has better resolution, than the model in mlb and soccer_intl; a measured gap is reported, not a mechanism.

sections.heading: How to read this on the site

blocks.text: The cross-sport-comparability inspector is built directly on kernel_transfer.json and is the place to check, before reading any number across sports on this site, whether a given sport/market pair is one of the two marked reliability_comparable here or one of the three that are not. The score-decomposition inspector carries the underlying Murphy reliability and resolution detail for the two comparable rows (mlb and soccer_intl moneyline_ingame), and the calibration inspector carries the wider per-grain BSS context behind Table 3.

Table 2's scoreboard and the figure above are one view of the same paired-delta rows the cross_sport_scoreboard module renders directly; reading them alongside kernel_transfer.json's comparability table is the intended order -- check whether a sport/market pair is comparable first, then read its scoreboard or BSS numbers, rather than the reverse.
